newsitem.title: USA: Harold Ickes won't be riding off into sunset.
newsitem.headline: Harold Ickes won't be riding off into sunset.

text.p: Harold Ickes, a one-time cowboy, will not be ambling off into the sunset after riding herd on Denver summit arrangements for President Bill Clinton.

Ickes says he is in the process of trying to put together a political consultants' firm in Washington. He was the controversial deputy White House chief of staff who ran Clinton's re-election campaign from the West Wing.

It was a batch of campaign documents from Ickes that led to some of the most startling revelations about Democratic fund-raising activities last year, including Clinton's approval of using the Lincoln Bedroom as a perk for deep-pocket donors.
There seems little doubt that Ickes will be called to testify at Senate hearings that start next month into the fund-raising scandal.
The tall, lanky New Yorker, who worked as a cowboy out West between high school and college, said in a telephone interview he did not think the hearings would turn up much.
"I think it is no more than a flap and a pretty weak flap at that," he said. "We'll have to see what they do at the hearings, who they call (to testify)."
"Having been in the middle of it, my view is there is very very little there, and that the public is probably growing pretty weary of it. But the hearings, who can predict them?" he said.
Ickes wanted to be Clinton's second-term chief of staff, and was disappointed when Clinton passed over him to pick Erskine Bowles for the job. But Ickes insists he has no bad feelings toward Clinton.
The president subsequently chose him to direct arrangements for his second-term inauguration, and then again to run the Denver summit.
Indeed, they have been talking on the phone and Ickes was there to greet him when the president got off Air Force One in Denver on Thursday.

"I love the western United States," said Ickes, whose father of the same name was President Franklin Roosevelt's interior secretary and confidant. "It's been great fun just living out here for a few months."
Ickes said running the summit was challenging but much less difficult than a national Democratic convention or a presidential inauguration.
"On the other hand, you have eight different countries involved and that makes it more interesting and difficult," he said.
